name: Teaching models to generate code and formal proofs
gist: These papers focus on training models to write working code and mathematical proofs by combining language models with formal verification and specialized reasoning techniques.
explain: Most language modeling research focuses on open-ended tasks like writing essays or answering questions, where there are many valid answers. But writing code and mathematical proofs are different—the answer either works or it does not. Papers in this area teach models to generate code that actually runs and proofs that are logically sound. This requires combining language models with formal verification systems that check whether generated code compiles and runs correctly, or whether a proof follows valid logical rules. The model learns from feedback on correctness, which is much more precise than human judgment.

The challenge is that code and proofs have much stricter rules than natural language. A single typo breaks code, and a logical gap breaks a proof, which means there is no partial credit. Models trained on natural language have learned to be loose and approximate, which does not work here because approximate code does not run. Some papers add specialized training where models see many examples of correct code and proofs so they learn the stricter conventions. Others use symbolic reasoning tools alongside the language model—the language model generates a candidate solution and a formal system checks it. If it fails, the feedback is used to improve the model by showing exactly what was wrong. When feedback is precise and verifiable, the model learns much faster than learning from vague human preferences because the signal is clear.

The payoff is tools that can assist programmers and mathematicians by suggesting code and checking proofs. This is valuable because code generation is tedious and error-prone for humans, and mathematicians spend enormous time writing and checking proofs. Even models that are imperfect can save time by generating starting points that humans then refine. These models also demonstrate that language models can learn structured, precise behavior if given the right training setup, which raises the question of what other precise tasks can be learned the same way.

papers.title: Actions Speak Louder than Prompts: A Large-Scale Study of LLMs for Graph Inference
papers.contribution: Code generation mode achieves strongest overall performance with especially large gains on long-text or high-degree graphs, and flexibly shifts reliance to most informative input types.

papers.title: Automated Formalization via Conceptual Retrieval-Augmented LLMs
papers.contribution: Enables seamless integration into LLM-based autoformalizers with consistent improvements across miniF2F, ProofNet, and a newly proposed AdvancedMath benchmark.

papers.title: Code World Models for General Game Playing
papers.contribution: Code-generated world models enable verifiable planning, strategic depth via MCTS search, and better generalization to new games.

papers.title: How Powerful are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?
papers.contribution: Demonstrates specification generation remains formidable challenge and that test case-based formal reasoning offers more faithful and discriminative progress measure than proof-based approaches.

papers.title: Huxley-G\"odel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine
papers.contribution: Outperforms prior self-improving agent methods on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot while using less wall-clock time, surpassing SWE-agent on SWE-bench Lite.

papers.title: A Minimal Agent for Automated Theorem Proving
papers.contribution: Achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art systems while using significantly simpler architecture and a fraction of their cost.

papers.title: Automated Formal Proofs of Combinatorial Identities via Wilf–Zeilberger Guidance and LLMs
papers.contribution: Achieves 34% proof success rate on LCI-Test (100 classical combinatorial identities), outperforming DeepSeek-V3 and Goedel-Prover-V2, with improvements on CombiBench and PutnamBench-Comb.

papers.title: Beyond Problem Solving: UOJ-Bench for Evaluating Code Generation, Hacking, and Repair in Competitive Programming
papers.contribution: Under one-shot evaluation, models fail to identify errors in over 50% of incorrect submissions, but test-time scaling improves success to above 90% and discovers errors in 5% of full-score submissions.

papers.title: Editable Proof Sketch for Automated Theorem Proving
papers.contribution: Achieves 76.0% pass rate on FormalMath-Lite (+14.1% vs. DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B) while significantly reducing token overhead compared to Hilbert.

papers.title: NEMO: Execution-Aware Optimization Modeling via Autonomous Coding Agents
papers.contribution: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on nine optimization benchmarks with substantial margins on several datasets by treating autonomous coding agents as first-class abstractions.

papers.title: Rule2DRC: Benchmarking LLM Agents for DRC Script Synthesis with Execution-Guided Test Generation
papers.contribution: Benchmark enables execution-correct evaluation; SplitTester substantially improves Best-of-N selection performance via generated discriminative test cases.

papers.title: The Invisible Lottery: How Subtle Cues Steer Algorithm Choice in LLM Code Generation
papers.contribution: Documents large systematic shifts in algorithm-family distributions (up to 100 percentage points), largely consistent with cue semantics, with implications for performance and security.

papers.title: VCG-Bench: Towards A Unified Visual-Centric Benchmark for Structured Generation and Editing
papers.contribution: Reveals challenges faced by current VLMs in structured fidelity and instruction compliance through systematic evaluation.
